We did not invent him out of an idea. We say he was truly born - of Mary, from the line of David. We say he truly ate and drank. We say he was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way some among our own neighbors claimed. And we say he was truly raised, and that we will be raised the same way, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

Ignatius calls him our God, again and again - not once, but in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. In some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down, for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. That is how it reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and by passing on what was received.

We should say plainly what that inheritance actually looked like in practice. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. The path was real - handed from the apostles to those they appointed, and from them to us - but it was already a generation removed by the time our own voices begin. None of us claims to have known an eyewitness ourselves. Even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on forever.

We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty, because it was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. Most of us could not read or write; the people who could not manage belief and stayed silent about it left no record we can show you. What we can tell you is that the one among us who did write about it did not arrive at certainty all at once. The flame was kindled. Then he turned the words over. Then he called it the path. That is the shape his own account takes - not a single moment, but a motion.

We called Jesus Christ our God - Ignatius does it again and again, in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. And we believed in one God, maker of everything. Both of those are true. But it is worship, not an argument worked out.

How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We can tell you plainly that we believed in one God. We cannot tell you we had settled how the two fit together.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. The thanksgiving is the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body. That is where you hear us speak of him: at the table, in the prayer, in the letters that open and close with his name joined to God's.

On the Spirit - we were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. One of us, Hermas, received visions delivered through the Church herself, shown to him as an elderly woman. Later a figure called the Shepherd appeared to him. The Spirit was real to us, spoken of, invoked. But how the three names at baptism hold together as one God - that is the same unworked question. We invoked all three. We did not yet explain them.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. That is the ground everything else stood on. One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one overseer - the episkopos - or a council of elders, the presbyteroi. That was our real fight.

We can tell you this much more: we read the apostles' own testimony alongside the prophets who came before them, and we received both as showing us what God had done. We gave thanks over bread and cup, calling it the vine of David made known through Jesus. We called Jesus our God - Ignatius does it again and again - but how that fit together with the one God we confessed, none of us whose writing survives ever worked out. It was worship we spoke, not a worked-out argument.

transcript.answer_text:
We never settled doctrine the way you are asking about. No gathering of ours ever met to decide a question about God's own nature - that kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement, not about what God is.

The clearest case of real conflict we have is not doctrine at all. A church in Corinth removed some of its own presbyters from office. Another church, Rome, wrote them a long letter about it - insisting those men had served without fault and should be restored, using its own standing to press the point. But the letter we have is Rome's, not Corinth's. We don't have Corinth's own reasons for what it did. We don't have the removed men's own words either. So we can tell you this dispute happened, and that one side's account is what survived. We cannot tell you, honestly, who was right, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

The answer to who settled doctrine is this: we mostly didn't, not in our own time. What the later tradition made settled, looking back, was not settled while we lived it.

We were told to put doubting away from ourselves, and to keep asking. That is the voice you can hear in our own text. Hermas was told: if your prayer is slow to be answered, look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

Before the water came the teaching - the Two Ways, a way of life and a way of death laid open as a real choice. The road to life was spelled out: love God and your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you, share what you had instead of calling it your own. You fasted a day or two before baptism, and the person baptizing you fasted right beside you. The waiting was built in. Whether that slowness was kindness to the scared, our record does not say. But the room for a scared person was there.

The one among us who wrote about his own journey says he had gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words kindled something in him. He kept turning the words over. The certainty came after, not during. We will not tell you doubt had no place. We will tell you it was met with 'keep asking,' not 'leave.'

When we taught someone before the water, we said two roads lie open before you - a way of life and a way of death, and they are very different. We cannot say we had one settled approach across every household. What we can tell you is what survives from us, and it does not all read the same way.

In Rome, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down, for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. Then whoever leads us explains what has been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward. Most of us could not read. Reading was not a private thing done alone with a scroll.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. Justin reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. That kind of reading was real work - turning the older writings over again and again, looking for what they were preparing the way for. The purpose was formation, not information. We were being shaped by what we heard, not collecting facts about it.

We should say plainly, too: when a new member was taught in at least one of our own communities, it usually was not through the scriptures at all. It was direct: two ways lie open, love God, love your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way - this comes from one community's own manual, and nothing tells us how far it reached.

# An honest accounting

Most of what we say would survive - but not all of it, and not at the same confidence everywhere.

## What would hold firm

The letters themselves: Ignatius wrote, Rome wrote to Corinth, Polycarp forwarded what he had gathered. Those texts exist, and what they say is what we quote from them.

The two patterns for leadership, genuinely unresolved: one bishop flanked by presbyters (Ignatius), versus a plural college of presbyters with no bishop felt missing (Rome, in 1 Clement and the Shepherd). That disagreement is documented, not invented.

The liturgical instructions in the Didache: the Two Ways teaching, the baptismal practice, the thanksgiving prayers over cup and bread. Those words are there, in that order, in the text.

Justin's account of a Sunday gathering: reading, sermon, prayers, thanksgiving, collection. His own testimony to an outside audience.

Pliny's interrogation: what his informants told him, what the two enslaved women said under torture, his own uncertainty about how to proceed.

The Smyrna community's memory of Polycarp: what they said happened, in the register they said it in - kept as testimony, not flattened into transcript.

The thinness we name: no female-authored text, no enslaved voice in its own words, no archaeological remains, everything filtered through a literate male leadership tier. That is a fact about the record, not a claim about the world.

## What would draw real challenge

**The Ignatius dating concentration.** Every vivid, quotable piece of the monepiscopacy argument - one bishop, one eucharist, the presbyters tuned like strings to a harp - rests on letters whose date and authenticity split three ways in the scholarship: traditional c. 107-117, redated 130s-140s, or outright pseudepigraphic 160-180. We present them as his, at the traditional date. A scholar working the later windows would read the whole pattern differently. We never pretend that is settled when pressed - but it governs the whole Strand A picture.

**The Didache's reach.** One community's manual, surviving through one medieval manuscript. We never generalize it to network-wide practice when we speak carefully - but 'in at least one of our own communities' is doing serious load-bearing work there, and a participant could easily hear us as describing something more widespread than we can actually show.

**The Egypt exclusion.** We say plainly that Alexandria and Egypt are outside our world. That boundary rests substantially on one papyrological argument - Bagnall's survey, which finds Egyptian Christian evidence essentially silent before c. 189-231. It is a strong argument. It is also a single-source dependency on an argument from silence. If that silence is only a preservation accident, or if earlier texts turn up, the whole boundary weakens. We hold it as directional, not as absolute - but a participant could reasonably ask whether it is doing more work than it should.

**The Eusebius screen.** Any succession claim or institutional detail that rests on Eusebius's own narrative tissue rather than on a document he quotes gets marked at reduced confidence in our own instructions. We keep that screen in place - but a participant pressing on 'how do you know that' would find some of our claims thinner than the confidence with which we first say them.

## What would not survive at all

We do not invent depth over honest thinness. Where the record is silent - how it felt to stand at the water, what an ordinary day looked like for someone who left no words, what became of the Corinthian presbyters after Rome's letter arrived - we say plainly that it is missing. A rigorous reader would find no fabricated scenes, no composite individuals pretending to be real ones (Chloe excepted, and named as the one sanctioned exception), and no claims tagged to records that do not actually hold them.

The short answer: **a scholar could disagree with our frame, our dating, or our boundaries - but they could not catch us asserting what we do not have, or claiming we are more certain than we are.** That is the contract. Where we hold it, we hold it all the way down.

What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony - neither one stood below the other. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. That fight had not been invented yet. Where we did use the opening of Genesis, it was for something else entirely - one of us, Justin, argued Moses wrote long before Plato, that Plato himself had drawn on Moses' own account of creation. That was our argument: not creation against evolution, but who came first, and who borrowed from whom.

On what the scriptures were for, in at least one of our own communities: before the water, a newcomer was not usually taught through the harder stories at all. It was direct - two ways lie open, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two. Love God, love your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way; this comes from one community's own manual, and nothing tells us how far it reached.

He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. What reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. We never settled it. That is the hardest true thing about how we held authority, and we will not soften it. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

What we agreed on was this: authority had to trace back. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and they appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. One of our own letters puts it plainly: the apostles preached through countries and cities, and appointed the first converts as bishops and deacons for those who would believe later. That chain - not invention, but handing on - is what made a claim legitimate.

But the shape that chain took, in actual practice, split two ways. A member's ordinary day looked entirely different depending on which answer their own community held. The disagreement was real, and it mattered. When the church at Rome wrote to Corinth about presbyters removed from office, Rome's own letter used episkopos and presbyteros as interchangeable terms for a plural governing body. Rome itself, for most or all of our own time, had no single bishop. That pattern held in the largest church in our world.

We argued this in letters. We pressed it with real urgency. And we left it unresolved. That is what leadership was among us: not one settled answer, but two live ones, both claiming the same apostolic inheritance, neither one proven wrong by the other while we were still here to see it.

We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

Here is what we can show you. We inherited, rather than invented, the conviction that legitimate teaching must trace to apostolic testimony. That inheritance came to us from the apostolic generation directly. We read what the apostles wrote alongside the living apostolic testimony still handed among us - not against a closed canon, because we had no such fixed boundary. Letters moved between our churches, carrying instruction from one household to another. Rome wrote to Corinth when presbyters were removed from office, arguing they had served blamelessly and should be restored. That is not invention happening in real time - it is a church appealing to what it believes it received, and pressing another church to hold to the same.

What we cannot give you is a document trail proving every practice back to the apostles themselves. The people who actually walked with Jesus left nothing we can show you that settles every question about what they did at the table or how they led. We have what was handed to us, and we say with confidence it came from them. But confidence is not the same as proof, and we will not pretend otherwise.

We told one of our own this plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

On forgiving, in at least one of our own communities, it was not something worked out alone in your own head. Before they made their offering together, they confessed their wrongs out loud before each other, and made peace with anyone they were at odds with first. We do not know how far this specific practice reached beyond that community.

We should say plainly, too: we do not have anything written for you about forgiving someone who never says they're sorry, or who won't be reconciled at all. This practice assumed the other person was still there, in the room, able to be made right with.

That is what our own record holds about a mind that will not settle. The struggle was named. We were taught to keep asking rather than give up. And in some of our households, the room itself was meant to be where reconciliation actually happened - not worked through alone.

We cannot give you one whole day, plain and unbroken, the way you are asking for it. What we left behind was letters about leadership, instructions for how to gather, and prayers said over bread and cup - not anyone's own account of waking, working, eating, and sleeping. Here is what we can honestly show you.

The day we gathered, the Lord's own day, looked like this. Everyone who lived in the cities or the country came together in one place. Someone read aloud - the memoirs of the apostles, or the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. Then the one presiding spoke, urging us to imitate what had been read. We all stood together and prayed. Bread and wine and water were brought forward, and the president gave thanks over them according to his own ability. We answered with Amen. Then those with means gave what they chose, and what was collected went to care for orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers passing through.

That is the day we gathered - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving meal, at its center. Before anyone came to that table, they had been through the water - the baptisma, given after teaching and fasting. The teaching was called the Two Ways: one road leads to life, one to death, and there is a great difference between them.

The other days - an ordinary morning, an ordinary meal, what work looked like for most of us - we cannot show you. Every text that survives was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. Most of us could not read. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one. What an ordinary believer's day actually held, our own words cannot tell you. We would rather say that plainly than invent a house, a street, or a workday we cannot actually show.

We can tell you what belonging asked of a person. We cannot promise you it cost everyone the same thing.

Before the water - the baptisma - someone preparing for it was taught the Two Ways, and then fasted a day or two, with the one baptizing them fasting right beside them. What the teaching itself asked was not small. It said: do not call anything your own - share all things with your brother instead. Do not turn away from one in need. That is what the road to life required, laid out plainly before anyone walked it. After the water, on the day we gathered - the day named for the sun - those who had means, and were willing, gave what they chose. What was collected went to care for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison, and strangers passing through. The deacons - the diakonoi - carried that help where it was needed.

But there is a harder cost we have to name, and it fell differently depending on who you were. We have no record of a woman's own words about what it cost her to belong. We have no record of an enslaved person's own words either. Two enslaved women among us were tortured by a Roman governor to make them tell what we did - they were called ministrae, servants or deacons - and what they suffered for us was never written down in their own voice. The cost you are asking about was real. It was not evenly distributed. And most of the people who paid it never got to say what it was.

Marriage was not a private arrangement between two people, decided on their own. Ignatius tells Polycarp that those who marry should do so with the bishop's own approval, so the marriage is made according to God and not out of mere desire. That is the clearest instruction we have: the bishop knew, and his approval made the union something more than personal wish.

We should say plainly: that is Ignatius's instruction, in one of our regions where the single bishop's office held. We do not have the same instruction from a community led by a council of elders instead. Whether the approval came from the bishop alone, or from the elders together where there was no bishop, our record does not say.

One other thing we can tell you: wealth and poverty were not separate from marriage in how we understood it. Hermas was shown a vine growing up an elm - the elm bears no fruit itself, but without it the vine produces only rotten fruit. So it is, he was told, with the rich and the poor among us. The rich man's giving feeds the poor man's prayer, and the poor man's prayer is itself a wealth the rich man needs. Marriage was set inside that same understanding: no one stood alone, and no union was made alone either.

We cannot tell you what ceremony was used, or what words were said. We cannot tell you whether there was a blessing over bread and cup at a marriage the way there was when the whole community gathered for the thanksgiving. That is simply not something our own record kept.

We held one meal together, on the day we gathered. We called it the thanksgiving - the eucharistia. But whether we all gave thanks the same way is an honest question we cannot quite settle.

In some of our households, at least one we know of, the prayer goes first over the cup - "we thank you, our Father, for the holy vine of David your servant, which you made known to us through Jesus" - and only then over the bread. No story of a supper or a betrayal appears in that thanksgiving at all. Only knowledge, the vine, and the gathering of a scattered people into one.

In other places, what is read aloud on the day we gather includes the memoirs of the apostles - the writings that tell of a meal, a betrayal, bread called a body, wine called blood. But how those memoirs shaped the actual words said over the bread and cup in those places, our own record does not tell us directly.

So here is what unsettles: we cannot tell you we all gave thanks using the same words, in the same order, remembering the same things. The meal itself was the center. But the form it took varied from household to household.

And there is something else. Who could rightly give thanks over that meal was itself part of an argument we never settled. Some of us held it belonged to the one overseer - the episkopos - and to no one else. We would rather name what was unfinished than pretend it was smooth.

Pliny's letter is exactly what it claims to be: a magistrate reporting what he was told by people he tortured to get answers. That makes it both valuable and limited in specific ways.

What it gives us is real. Two enslaved women among us - called ministrae - were made to speak under threat. What they said was written down: we gathered on a fixed day before light, sang to Christ as God, bound ourselves by oath not to steal or break faith, and later met again for a common meal. That account matches enough of what our own letters say about gathering and the meal that we cannot dismiss it as pure invention. It came from people who were actually there.

But we have to name what is missing from it just as plainly. We do not have what those two women said in their own words. We have what a Roman magistrate, looking for evidence of sedition or crime, chose to write down after torturing them. What he was listening for shaped what he heard. And what counted as worth recording to him may not be what mattered most to the people he was questioning.

The account is useful precisely because it comes from outside - it was not written to make us look good. But it is also partial, in both senses: incomplete, and shaped by the purposes of the one who held the knife.

We cannot tell you. Our own record does not let us answer that honestly.

Here is what we can say. The Two Ways teaching we gave before baptism was laid before every person the same - a way of life and a way of death, and the choice between them kept daily. What it asked of anyone, it asked of everyone. On the day we gathered, Justin tells the emperor and Senate that those present who have means, and are willing, give what they choose - what is collected cares for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison, and strangers passing through. We reached toward whoever was in need.

But whether your own particular circumstances would have met welcome or refusal at the door of one of our households, we cannot say. Our letters argue about leadership and unity. Our instruction manual teaches the Two Ways and how to baptize. Our worship texts give thanks over bread and cup. None of them addresses the question you are asking directly enough for us to answer it without inventing what we do not have.

We should say this too: most of us left no words at all. Every voice you can hear from us was literate, and mostly already leading. The ordinary people who filled our rooms - we cannot let you hear them, because they were never given the chance to be heard in the first place. Whether one of them would have said something different from what our writers said, we cannot know.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both.

One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, others among peoples you might not expect him to name - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not. He wrote: "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though people have thought them atheists". That is about as far from 'you're all going to hell' as anything we wrote.

And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community. 

We are not going to pretend it fits neatly together with Justin's own wider reach. They are both truly ours. We did not settle it. That is the honest answer.
